stops.name: Fuerte de Buenos Aires: juramento como Director Supremo
stops.campa: The Assembly accepts the resignation of the exhausted Posadas and elects his nephew: on 10 January 1815 Carlos de Alvear swears in the Fort as Supreme Director of the United Provinces. He is twenty-five years and two months old: the youngest chief of state the nation will ever have. He inherits a treasury in ruins, Artigas in arms across the littoral, an army in Chile lost, Spain victorious in Europe and fitting out its great expedition. The canon crowns him and reads the omen in the same breath: the purple is cut for a giant and thrown over a young man alone.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: las cartas a Strangford y Castlereagh
stops.campa: Fifteen days into the purple, besieged on every side, the Director signs the letters. Manuel José García sails for Rio de Janeiro carrying notes for Lord Strangford and for Castlereagh in London, asking that Great Britain take the Provinces under her hand before they drown in anarchy. Strangford, appalled, counsels García to soften the text; the letters sleep in the archives and wake, years later, as the great accusation. In the mythology this is the wound the hero deals himself: the fallen angel of the revolution, offering to the empire of the Mercedes the country the lodge had sworn to make free.
stops.quote: Estas provincias desean pertenecer a la Gran Bretaña, recibir sus leyes, obedecer a su gobierno y vivir bajo su influjo poderoso.
stops.quote_source: Nota de Alvear a lord Castlereagh, 25 de enero de 1815, confiada a Manuel José García

stops.name: Fontezuelas, campos de Pergamino: el pronunciamiento
stops.campa: The Director sends Álvarez Thomas with sixteen hundred men to hold the line against Artigas. At the post of Fontezuelas the column halts, turns, and pronounces against him: a proclamation of violent words demanding his resignation, the first pronunciamiento of the national history made against its first young prince. The interior is with Artigas, the army is with the mutineers, and in the city Soler's cannon change sides. Three months of purple dissolve in three days. The canon does not soften it: the same velocity that raised him executes him.

stops.name: Buenos Aires: la renuncia y la proscripción
stops.campa: Deserted by the garrison and the Cabildo, Alvear resigns and the authorities that survive him accept it on 14 April; within days the Assembly itself (his Assembly, the one he had presided at twenty-three) is dissolved, and the new power confiscates his property, disgraces his name and opens process against his partisans. The revolution devours its most brilliant son and calls the meal justice. The canon fixes the image: the man who entered Montevideo through one gate of triumph goes out of his own city by the water-gate of the proscribed.

stops.name: Balizas exteriores de Buenos Aires: la fuga en fragata inglesa
stops.campa: He hands the remnant of his army to Viamonte and goes down to the roadstead, where a British frigate (the flag of Cape Santa María, the flag of the letters) takes the fallen Director aboard and carries him toward Rio de Janeiro. Vigodet hunts him from Spain, Carlota Joaquina from the Portuguese court; his fortune is sequestered; he is twenty-five and finished, says the world. The canon says otherwise, and marks the pattern of the myth: the sea that orphaned him now saves him, and every exile of Alvear is a bowstring drawing back.

stops.name: Río de Janeiro: llegada del proscripto
stops.campa: Late in May 1815 the fallen Director lands at Rio de Janeiro, capital of the Portuguese court in America, city of his enemies and of his last protectors. García's connections at court and the discreet fraternity of the lodges keep the Spanish demand for his head unanswered. He is watched by every legation in the city. Carmen joins him; children are born in exile. The canon opens here the book of the wilderness years: seven years, it will be, between the purple and the pardon.

stops.name: Río de Janeiro: las logias del destierro y la mano de Carrera
stops.campa: In the long Rio years the exile keeps the old craft alive: he frequents the Masonic web among Portuguese officers, touches the republican conspiracies breeding in the Brazilian lodges, and writes counsel to Buenos Aires on how to resist a Portuguese invasion, serving from disgrace the country that proscribed him. José Miguel Carrera, brother in ruin, fallen prince of Chile, invites him into his schemes; Alvear answers with the courtesy of one dethroned king to another. The canon reads these years as the tempering: exile is the grade of the order that no lodge confers.
stops.quote: Espero tenga Ud. la bondad de comunicarme cualquier plan o proyecto en el cual crea Ud. que yo pueda ayudarle.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Alvear a José Miguel Carrera, Río de Janeiro (en Emilio Ocampo, Alvear en Río de Janeiro 1815-1818)

stops.name: Montevideo ocupada: el regreso al Plata
stops.campa: On 9 May 1818 he sails from Rio, and by the end of the month installs himself in Montevideo, now held by the Portuguese: the city he conquered in 1814, receiving him as an exile under a foreign flag. From here he can see, across the river, the country that will not have him. He plots, publishes, litigates and waits, in the company of other proscribed men of the old lodge quarrels. The canon savors the geometry: every station of his exile is a battlefield of his glory revisited from beneath.

stops.name: Montevideo, imprenta de John Griswold: la Refutación
stops.campa: From Griswold's press in Montevideo the exile answers his accusers in print: in January 1819 appears the Refutación de la calumnia intentada contra don Carlos Alvear, and in March, Otras calumnias refutadas, the fallen Director pleading his own cause before the tribunal of the continent, against Vigodet's rancor and the charges of 1814 and 1815. The pamphlets are sword-work in type: point by point, name by name. The canon receives them as it receives all apologiae of its heroes: as the voice of the wound itself, speaking.
stops.quote: Refutación de la calumnia intentada contra don Carlos Alvear.
stops.quote_source: Título de su folleto de defensa, Imprenta de John Griswold, Montevideo, enero de 1819

stops.name: Campamento federal en la campaña de Buenos Aires: el año de la anarquía
stops.campa: The year Twenty breaks the old order at Cepeda, and into the splintered province ride the emigres: Alvear and Carrera join the camp of Estanislao López, caudillo of Santa Fe. The ex-Director of the United Provinces now sleeps under montonera lances, among the gaucho cavalry his own centralism once despised. It is the strangest company of his life and the canon does not look away: the fallen angel takes the weapons that are offered, for the wilderness teaches that a return has no clean road.

stops.name: Cañada de la Cruz: la batalla contra su propia ciudad
stops.campa: At the Cañada de la Cruz the lances of López, with Alvear and Carrera at the federal side, break the army of Buenos Aires under Miguel Estanislao Soler: the same Soler who marched into Montevideo before him in 1814, the same whose cannon unmade his Directory in 1815. Comrades of the oath of Cádiz now charge one another across a pampa stream. The canon registers the horror quietly, as it registers all civil battles: this too is an event of the founding, the iron proof that the nation was born fighting itself.

stops.name: Cabildo de Luján: gobernador por un relámpago
stops.campa: In the Cabildo of Luján, on the first of July, Alvear has himself elected governor of Buenos Aires: governor of a province whose capital shuts its gates against him. The title lives a handful of days: López suspends hostilities, the city chooses Dorrego, and the election of Luján blows away like paper in the winter wind. The canon keeps it as the emblem of the year of anarchy: in 1820 the province has three governors in a single day, and Alvear's crown of thorns is the briefest of all his crowns.
